rv.q: Toss in a couple of solid performances from younger Brits Dylan and Horn – he is particularly good as a brittle, obnoxious Nick – and you've got something very special.
Both bring tremendous star power to an absolute knock-out evening.
This is a chance to see two actors at the top of their game, and at exhaustive, almost exhausting length.
For all the comedy and nervous laughs, this couple does combust and the end is devastating.
This is theatre of the highest calibre: intelligent, exhilarating and emotionally shattering.
It is a great night at the theatre.
It’s inevitable that any attempt to mount a production of WHO’S AFRAID OF VIRGINIA WOOLF will draw comparisons with Richard Burton and Elizabeth Taylor’s 1966 movie.

Marianne Elliott's rich and propulsive new production of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf @sohoplace skillfully avoids the quicksand, ensuring the audience live through the wreckage alongside the characters as we're all invited to an afterparty with Martha and George.
It's a baffling 3 hours and 20 minutes in the theatre, and I am afraid to say there are better ways to spend that time.

cn.t: Anderson and Crudup deliver towering performances in Elliott's revelatory production of Albee's classic, which feels fresh and intimate rather than dated. Critics praise the softer, comedic approach that makes the shock moments land even harder.
